newsitem.title: ITALY: Foreign investors concerned over Olivetti.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors concerned over Olivetti.

text.p: Nearly a year after information technology group Olivetti launched a rights issue in a bid to turn round the business, foreign investors feel they are being kept in the dark by the company, analysts said on Friday.

"Shareholders do not feel that they are being told what is going on," said Tim Hirst, a telecommunications industry analyst with Kleinwort Benson in London. "People just don't believe the company's press releases any more."

Frustration with Olivetti -- a high-flying stock on Milan's stock exchange throughout the 1980s -- has focused on the group's ailing personal computer division, which has piled up heavy losses for several years.

The company said at the beginning of July that the PC business had broken even in the second quarter of 1996 but analysts are still sceptical as they nervously await a full first-half report to be published on September 26.

A group of foreign institutional investors representing around 25 percent of Olivetti's stock met in London at the beginning of the week to discuss ways of forcing Olivetti to boost the value of its shares, which have languished for months.

One London-based stockbroker, who asked not to be named, said he believed the investors were pondering whether to call an extraordinary assembly, which would require the backing of at least one fifth of Olivetti's stockholders.
Around 70 percent of Olivetti's shares are now in the hands of foreign investors.

Industry watchers say Olivetti should get out of the PC business all together so it can focus its energies on its fast-growing mobile phone venture, Omnitel Pronto Italia, and on developing other telecommunications interests.

The investor group is also reported to have demanded a meeting with Olivetti's new chief executive officer, Francesco Caio, and to want clarification of the role played in the running of the company by its chairman Carlo De Benedetti.

One analyst said the investors appeared to lack a clear strategy. "They want to make themselves known to the management and they will threaten to call an extraordinary shareholders' meeting. This is very preliminary," said the London analyst.

Many investors believe that De Benedetti, who transformed the company from an ailing typewriter maker into a thriving PC business in the early 1980s, should detach himself from the management of Olivetti even though he retains a stake in group.
A spokeswoman for Olivetti, Flavia Carraro, said that Caio planned to hold meetings with investors in the near future.
"From now on there will be a series of meetings between management and key shareholders, although nothing has been scheduled yet," said Carraro.
Olivetti, which has not broken even since 1990, made a record loss of 1.589 trillion ($1.05 billion) last year.

Olivetti made a 2.26 trillion lire ($1.05 billion) rights issue in October 1995 as part of a sweeping restructuring programme which involved job cuts and the hiving off of the PC division into a separate company.
"People do not believe the money raised (by the rights issue) has been used to fix the problem," said Hirst. "Shareholder cash has been sucked into the PC business."
Another source of grievance was the sudden unexplained departure two months ago of Corrado Passera, the group managing director seen as a driving force behind the restructuring plan .
Olivetti's shares have dropped steadily since the cash call and were trading on Friday afternoon at 793 lire -- well below their par value of 1,000 lire.

One industry-watcher said Caio needed more time to take hold of the company, while De Benedetti's influence was on the wane. "His (De Benedetti's) grip on the company has clearly lessened. Caio is calling the shots and one has to have time to see what his strategy is going to be," said Ian Macleod at Natwest Securities in Paris.
